o: Put elements whose index is prime into A, the rest into B, and return |sum(A) − sum(B)|. Example 1: index 2 is prime → A={4}, B={2,3} → 1. Example 2: indices 2,3 prime → |7 − 4| = 3. Indices can be negative-valued elements, so keep sums in 64-bit types. Sieve indices up to n−1 once.
k: Primality of the index, not the value, decides placement.
Values reach ±10⁹ with n up to 10⁵, so sums need 64-bit integers.
A simple sieve of Eratosthenes over [0, n) is the natural preprocessing.

a.i: Mark composites among indices 0..n−1 with a sieve, then accumulate two sums in one pass and return the absolute difference.
s: Build boolean sieve over indices 0..n−1 (0 and 1 not prime).
Accumulate sumA for prime indices, sumB otherwise.
a.t: O(n log log n) — sieve dominates the single accumulation pass.

a.i: Skip the sieve and test each index for primality by trial division up to √index. Slightly slower asymptotically but needs no auxiliary array and is trivially correct.
s: Write isPrime(i) checking divisibility by 2 and odd d up to √i.
For each index, add its value to sumA or sumB.
a.t: O(n√n) worst case — √i trial division per index; fine for n = 10⁵.

w: Use the sieve — it is the canonical tool and faster. Only real pitfall is 32-bit overflow of the sums in C++/Java (values ±10⁹ × 10⁵ elements). Follow-up: split by indices that are primes of a special form, or return both subarrays.
